answer: The premise is incorrect. node2vec does not use genetic algorithms, tournament selection, chromosome crossover, bit-flip mutation, or any fitness function. It is not evolutionary and has no genetic optimization step. node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016) learns node embeddings in two stages. First, it generates node sequences with second-order biased random walks, controlled by return parameter p and in-out parameter q, which interpolate between breadth-first and depth-first style exploration. Second, it feeds these sequences to a skip-gram model with negative sampling, as in word2vec. The embeddings are fit by maximizing the log-probability of observing each node's neighborhood context, approximated with negative sampling, and this is optimized with stochastic gradient descent (asynchronous SGD). The objective is a gradient-based likelihood, not a fitness function. If a genetic-algorithm variant of node embedding is intended, it would be a different method from node2vec.
confidence_reasoning: I am confident node2vec uses biased random walks with skip-gram and SGD and has no genetic algorithm component, though I have not checked the paper text directly for every detail such as the exact optimizer naming.
